827.title: Micah: what is good (Micah 6:8)
827.hook: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God"
827.howItsDone: Micah 6:8 is read in synagogue at the end of a prophetic reading from Micah, and it is quoted in Jewish teaching on justice and kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah sulked outside Nineveh over a withered plant, and the book ended on God's question. Your line was doest thou well to be angry. Where did a little pity find its way out of you? Today, another of the Twelve, and an answer short enough to carry in a pocket. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

The sixth chapter of Micah opens like a courtroom, and the mountains are the jury. In the King James: "Hear ye, O mountains, the LORD's controversy." God makes the case: I brought you up out of Egypt, I sent you Moses and Aaron and Miriam. What have I done to you? And the people, put on the spot, start bidding. Shall we come with burnt offerings? With calves a year old? Would thousands of rams do it? Rivers of oil, ten thousand of them? Then the worst bid of all: shall I give my firstborn for my sin? Each offer bigger, and more desperate, than the one before. And then a voice cuts in, and the answer is small.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINS ARE THE JURY.` → `RAMS, RIVERS OF OIL, A FIRSTBORN?` → `THE ANSWER IS SMALL.`

segments.voice: It begins: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good." Shown already. Not a secret. Not a new demand. Then: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God." Three verbs, and each points a different way. Do justly points outward, at how you treat people. The Hebrew is mishpat: justice, a fair ruling, the thing a good judge does at the city gate. It's something done with your hands, at work and in the market. Love mercy points inward, at what you want. The Hebrew word behind mercy is chesed, the steady, loyal kindness that goes past what's owed. And notice the verb. Micah doesn't say do mercy. He says love it. Some readers hear the difference this way: justice can be done even through gritted teeth, but chesed has to be wanted. Walk humbly points alongside. Not a leap. Not a performance. A walk, at walking pace, with God. English translations render that Hebrew phrase in more than one way, humbly or modestly, but either way it's quiet. Now look at what the answer does to the bidding war. The people kept raising the price, rams, rivers, a child, as if the right gift could stand in for a fairer life. Micah's answer isn't a bigger offering. It's a different kind of thing altogether: a way of living, with people and with God, on an ordinary weekday. That doesn't throw out the offerings or the Torah; two chapters earlier, Micah pictures the nations climbing to the Temple mountain to learn it. The answer asks that the life match the gift. Justly, mercy, humbly. You can do all three before dinner.
screen: `SHOWN ALREADY, NOT A SECRET.` · `DO JUSTLY: MISHPAT, A FAIR RULING.` · `LOVE MERCY: CHESED, WANTED, NOT JUST DONE.` · then, large: `WALK HUMBLY WITH THY GOD.` · then: `NOT A BIGGER GIFT, A DIFFERENT LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do all three, starting now, in small. Settle, and breathe. For do justly, find one place where something is a little unfair and your hand is in it: a chore unevenly split, credit not given, a message you owe someone. Name what fair would look like. For love mercy, bring to mind one person who owes you something, an apology, a favor, and notice whether any part of you wants to let it go. For walk humbly, just walk with the breath. In, and out, nothing to prove. If you pray, you can say the verse slowly, phrase by phrase. The bell holds the time.
Micah. A prophet of the Twelve, who answered a bidding war with three verbs: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Today's word.
Your line: justly, mercy, humbly. Today, do one of each before you sleep: one fair thing, one kindness nobody owed, one quiet thing nobody sees. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

828.title: Micah: under the fig tree (Micah 4:4)
828.hook: each under their vine and fig tree, "and none shall make them afraid"
828.howItsDone: Jews read Micah among the Twelve, and the hope of each person under their own vine and fig tree is sung and quoted in Jewish life as a picture of peace without fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Micah answered a bidding war of rams and rivers of oil with three verbs. Your line was justly, mercy, humbly. Which of the three came easiest? Today, Micah again, and a picture of peace small enough to sit in. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

A fig tree throws real shade. Its leaves are broad, and on a hot afternoon the ground under one is cool and green. Micah's fourth chapter starts enormous. The mountain of the LORD's house raised above the hills, and peoples streaming toward it to learn. Then the line about swords, in the King James: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks." Nation shall not lift up a sword against nation. That's the view from very high up. And then Micah does something unexpected. He comes all the way down, from nations to one person, sitting in one patch of shade.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN, AND PEOPLES STREAMING.` → `SWORDS INTO PLOWSHARES.` → `DOWN TO ONE PATCH OF SHADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse: "But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid." Read it slowly, because every piece is doing work. Sit. Not marching, not working, not standing guard. Sitting is what you do when you don't have to watch the road. His vine, his fig tree. His own. Not rented, not borrowed, not taken from someone else. The picture is of someone who expects to stay. And then the last phrase. In Hebrew it's short: ve'ein macharid, and none shall make them tremble. That's how Micah measures peace. Not by a treaty, not by a map with no battles on it, but by whether a person sitting in their own yard has anything left to flinch at. The swords are gone, yes. But the vision isn't finished until the fear is gone too. The picture has a past in the Bible. In the book of Kings, in Solomon's days, Judah and Israel are said to have lived safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree. So Micah's hope reaches back to a remembered good time and promises it again, for everyone. The verse ends with a signature: for the mouth of the LORD of hosts hath spoken it. And that brings it close to home. What makes people afraid is often small and close. A tone of voice. A door slammed. A person who might laugh at you. The vision is as big as the nations. Its last line fits in a kitchen.
screen: `SIT: NOBODY HAS TO WATCH THE ROAD.` · `HIS OWN VINE, HIS OWN FIG TREE.` · then, large: `AND NONE SHALL MAKE THEM AFRAID.` · then: `THE LAST LINE FITS IN A KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: make someone feel safe. Start with yourself. First, notice anything in you that's braced: shoulders up, jaw tight, waiting for the next thing. Let a little of it go, the way you would sitting in shade. Then bring to mind one person who might be braced around you. A child. A coworker who answers to you. A partner, a parent, a friend who seems careful lately. Ask what would let them sit easy in your company. A softer voice. A promise kept. Telling them plainly they're not in trouble. Choose one. If you pray, you can say Micah's line for them. The bell holds the time.
Micah. The prophet who brought the peace of nations down to one person under a vine and a fig tree, with nothing to be afraid of. Today's word.
Your line: none shall make them afraid. Today, be the reason one person flinches a little less: a gentler answer, a calmer text, a kept word. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

829.title: Habakkuk: by faithfulness (Habakkuk 2:4)
829.hook: the Talmud says Habakkuk reduced the whole Torah to one line: the righteous live by faith (Makkot 24a)
829.howItsDone: Jews read Habakkuk among the Twelve, and the Talmud's tractate Makkot names Habakkuk 2:4 as the single line on which the commandments stand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Micah brought the peace of nations down to one person in the shade of a fig tree. Your line was none shall make them afraid. Who sat a little easier near you? Today, a prophet who opens with a complaint. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

"O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" That's how Habakkuk begins, in the King James. Not with a message for the people, but with the prophet arguing upward. He sees violence and strife, the law gone slack, the wicked hemming in the righteous, and he asks why God lets him watch it. An answer comes, and it troubles him even more, so he asks again. And then he does something stubborn. He climbs up to wait: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower." He's not coming down until he hears back.
screen: `HOW LONG SHALL I CRY?` → `THE ANSWER TROUBLES HIM MORE.` → `UP THE TOWER, TO WAIT.`

segments.voice: The answer, when it comes, starts with instructions about handwriting. "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it." Big letters, so even someone running past can read them. Then a warning about time: "though it tarry, wait for it." And then the line: "the just shall live by his faith." The Hebrew word under faith is emunah. In English, faith can sound like something in your head, a belief you hold about a thing. Emunah leans toward something you do with your whole life: steadiness, firmness, keeping faith. The same word turns up in Exodus, when Moses holds up his arms through a long battle and Aaron and Hur prop them up. The King James says his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. Steady: that's the Hebrew emunah. So the righteous live by steadiness. And notice the small word his. His faithfulness. Some readers hear the righteous person's own steadiness. Others hear God's faithfulness, the thing the righteous lean on while they wait. The Hebrew can carry both. Now the Talmud. In tractate Makkot, Rabbi Simlai teaches that Moses was given six hundred thirteen commandments, and that later voices gathered them into fewer and fewer lines. David set them on eleven, Isaiah on six, Micah, the prophet of the last two days, on three, Isaiah again on two. For the last step the rabbis weigh Amos, then settle on this: Habakkuk came and set them all on one. The righteous shall live by his faith. Not a rule about food or Shabbat, but the ground every rule stands on. One line, written large enough to read on the run.
screen: `WRITE IT PLAIN, TO READ ON THE RUN.` · `THOUGH IT TARRY, WAIT FOR IT.` · then, large: `THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY HIS FAITH.` · then: `EMUNAH: STEADY HANDS TILL SUNSET.` · then: `ALL OF IT, SET ON ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: For the practice, live today by one trust. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you're waiting on: an answer, a result, a person to change, a door to open. Notice how waiting feels in your body. Then, like Habakkuk on the tower, choose to stand where you are rather than run. Pick one steady thing you can trust today: a person who has kept their word, a habit that holds you, or, if you pray, God's faithfulness. Breathe as if your arms were being held up. You can let Habakkuk's words ride the breath: though it tarry, wait for it. The bell holds the time.
Habakkuk. The prophet who argued, climbed the tower to wait, and heard the line the Talmud says holds up all the rest: the just shall live by his faith. Today's word.
Your line: live by faithfulness. Today, keep one small promise exactly as you made it, on time, and let that be your steadiness. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

830.title: Zechariah: not by might (Zechariah 4:6)
830.hook: read on Hanukkah: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit"
830.howItsDone: Jews read Zechariah's vision of the golden lampstand as the prophetic reading on the Shabbat of Hanukkah, and the line "not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit" is sung and quoted during the holiday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Habakkuk waited on his tower and heard one line that holds up the rest. Your line was live by faithfulness. Which promise did you keep, exactly as you made it? Today, a prophet shaken awake to see a lamp. Day eight hundred thirty.

The angel comes back and wakes him. In the King James, Zechariah says he was waked "as a man that is wakened out of his sleep." Groggy, he's asked what he sees. A lampstand, all of gold, with a bowl on top and seven lamps. And standing beside it, one on each side, two olive trees. Golden pipes run from the trees, so the oil flows straight to the light, and nobody has to carry a single jar. Zechariah asks the obvious thing: "What are these, my lord?" And the answer he gets doesn't sound like an answer at all.
screen: `SHAKEN AWAKE.` → `A GOLDEN LAMPSTAND, TWO OLIVE TREES.` → `WHAT ARE THESE, MY LORD?`

segments.voice: Instead of a key to the symbols, he's handed a message for someone else. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit, saith the LORD of hosts." The message is for Zerubbabel, a leader of the people who came back from exile in Babylon. His job is rebuilding the Temple in Jerusalem, and the chapter hints that the work looks too big. So the next line names the problem: "Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain." Whatever is piled in his way, a heap of rubble, a wall of opposition, a people too tired to begin, will be leveled. Not by an army. Then the promise, in plain building terms: "The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it." And then a question that is really a rebuke to the doubters: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" A foundation is small. A first stone is small. The people looking at it were tempted to scoff. Now put the vision back together. A lamp that's fed straight from living trees, with no one straining to haul the oil. Some readers hear that as the picture of the whole message: the light keeps burning, and it isn't muscle that keeps it lit. Jews read this passage in synagogue on the Shabbat of Hanukkah. A golden lamp, a holiday of lights, and, some hear, a reminder that what is celebrated was not, in the end, about might.
screen: `A MESSAGE FOR ZERUBBABEL.` · `O GREAT MOUNTAIN, BECOME A PLAIN.` · then, large: `NOT BY MIGHT, NOR BY POWER, BUT BY MY SPIRIT.` · then: `WHO HATH DESPISED THE DAY OF SMALL THINGS?` · then: `READ ON THE SHABBAT OF HANUKKAH.`

segments.voice: The practice today: solve one thing gently. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one problem you've been trying to win by force. An argument you keep pushing. A person you keep pressing. A project you're muscling through on willpower alone. Name your great mountain. Then ask what the small first stone would be. Not the whole solution. One gentle step: a question instead of a demand, a pause instead of a push, asking for help. Let your breath be the oil that flows without hauling: in, and out, no effort to make it happen. If you pray, you can hold Zechariah's line for a while. The bell holds the time.
Zechariah. The prophet who saw a golden lamp fed by two olive trees, and carried a message to a weary builder: not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit. Today's word.
Your line: not by might. Today, solve one thing gently: ask instead of insisting, lay one small stone instead of moving the whole mountain. Day eight hundred thirty.

831.title: Malachi: turn the hearts (Malachi 3:23–24)
831.hook: the last prophet: Elijah will turn parents' hearts to children, children's to parents
831.howItsDone: Malachi's closing verses are read in synagogue as a prophetic reading, including on the Shabbat before Passover, and by custom the verse promising Elijah is read again so the reading ends on hope.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zechariah's golden lamp, fed by two olive trees, and a message for a weary builder. Your line was not by might. What did you solve gently? Today, the last book of the Twelve, and its last lines. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

After all of it, the burning coal on Isaiah's lips, Jeremiah's broken jar, the valley of dry bones, Jonah in the sea, the books of the prophets end with a handful of short verses at the close of Malachi. First, a look back. In the King James: "Remember ye the law of Moses my servant." Then a look ahead: Elijah the prophet will be sent, before the great and terrible day of the LORD. And then the very last promise in the prophets. Of everything a prophet could hold out at the end, a rebuilt kingdom, defeated enemies, a world made new, Malachi chooses something much closer to home.
screen: `REMEMBER THE LAW OF MOSES.` → `ELIJAH WILL BE SENT.` → `THE LAST PROMISE IS CLOSE TO HOME.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." Read it once more and listen for the direction. It runs both ways. The Torah had already told children to honor their parents. This goes further. Parents turn too, and the parents are named first. Elijah's job, at the edge of the great day, isn't to win a battle. It's to get two generations facing each other again. Readers hear that in different ways. Some hear parents and children who've stopped understanding each other, and a promise that the gap will close. Some hear the generations of a people, the old ones who remember and the young ones who will carry it on, turned back toward the same Torah Malachi just told them to remember. It's the same Elijah who stood on Mount Carmel and went up in a whirlwind, and the same Elijah Jews welcome with a cup at the Passover table and sing about as Shabbat ends. Now, the hard part. The verse doesn't stop there. It goes on: turn the hearts, or the land will be struck with destruction. That's the last word of the book. And here's a custom. When Malachi is read aloud in synagogue, the reader doesn't stop on that harsh line. The custom is to go back and read the verse before it again, the promise of Elijah, so the prophets close on hope rather than ruin. Even in the reading, someone turns back toward the listener.
screen: `IT RUNS BOTH WAYS.` · `PARENTS ARE NAMED FIRST.` · then, large: `THE HEART OF THE FATHERS TO THE CHILDREN.` · then: `READ THE PROMISE AGAIN, END ON HOPE.`

segments.voice: Now the practice: reach across a generation. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone a generation away from you, older or younger. A parent or grandparent. A child, a niece, a nephew. An older neighbor, a young coworker. Notice whether your heart is turned toward them, or a little away. Then find one question you've never asked them about their life. What was hard at your age? What do you wish someone had told you? What are you into lately? Hold the question, and their face, for a while. If you pray, you can say Malachi's line with them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Malachi. The last book of the Twelve, which closes the prophets with Elijah turning the hearts of parents and children toward each other. Today's word.
Your line: turn the hearts. Today, reach one generation over: ask your question, and let the answer run longer than you planned. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

832.title: The Prophets close
832.hook: the Talmud says after the prophets, prophecy passed to the wise, and to children and fools (Bava Batra 12b)
832.howItsDone: Jews read from the Prophets in synagogue on Shabbat and festivals as the haftarah, and the Talmud's discussion of where prophecy went is studied as part of the tradition's own account of rabbinic learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malachi's last promise: Elijah turning the hearts of parents and children toward each other. Your line was turn the hearts. What did you ask across a generation, and what did you hear? Today, the prophets go quiet. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

Malachi rolls up, and the section of the Bible called the Prophets is done. This year opened it the day Moses died, with Joshua told to be strong. Since then: judges and kings, and prophets who argued, wept and waited, and the Twelve, from Hosea's broken marriage to Malachi's turning hearts. And then silence. The rabbis felt that silence, and they asked a question about it. When the prophets stop, where does the voice go? Their answer, in the Talmud's tractate Bava Batra, has a surprise at the end.
screen: `MALACHI ROLLS UP.` → `JOSHUA TO MALACHI.` → `WHERE DOES THE VOICE GO?`

segments.voice: Here is the passage, retold. Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa teaches: from the day the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to the wise. The Talmud pushes back right away: isn't a sage a prophet too? It answers that prophecy was taken from the prophets, but not from the wise. Then a teacher named Amemar adds: the sage is greater than the prophet. That's a bold thing to say, and it tells you how the rabbis saw their own work. The voice didn't vanish. It moved into study: into people sitting with these very books, arguing over a verse, asking what it asks of us now. Every one of these days, from Micah's three verbs to Habakkuk's one line, has been that kind of listening. Then comes the surprise. Rabbi Yochanan says: from the day the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to fools and to children. The Talmud even tells a story of a passing remark, from someone nobody took seriously, that turned out to be true. Readers have heard this in more than one way. Some hear a joke with an edge: these days, prophecy is so cheapened that only fools speak it. Others hear something tender: the truth now turns up where nobody guards it. A child says the thing every adult in the room was too careful to say. A stranger's offhand line answers the question you've carried for a month. Both readings agree on this much. The prophets close, but listening doesn't. The scrolls are finished. The people reading them, arguing over them, and sometimes hearing a true word from the least likely mouth in the room, are not.
screen: `GIVEN TO THE WISE.` · `THE SAGE IS GREATER THAN THE PROPHET.` · then, large: `GIVEN TO FOOLS AND TO CHILDREN.` · then: `THE PROPHETS CLOSE, LISTENING DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: For today's practice, listen for wisdom from a child. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something a child once said that stopped you. A question you couldn't answer. A blunt truth at the dinner table. A small kindness they didn't know was big. If no child comes to mind, think of someone you don't usually listen to, and something they said that turned out right. Hold their words for a while. Then just listen to the room around you, the small sounds nobody guards, for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can let the listening be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Bava Batra, the Talmud tractate where the rabbis say that when the Prophets closed, their voice passed to the wise, and to fools and children. Today's word.
Your line: the voice goes on. Today, listen to one child, or one person you usually talk over, all the way to the end of their sentence. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

833.title: The Writings
833.hook: the third part of the Tanakh: poems, wisdom books and stories
833.carry: they praise, they doubt, they complain
833.howItsDone: Jews pray the Psalms daily in the synagogue service and read the short scrolls of the Writings at their festivals, such as Esther on Purim and Ruth on Shavuot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prophets closed, and in tractate Bava Batra the rabbis said the voice passed to the wise, and to fools and children. Your line was the voice goes on. Whose sentence did you hear all the way to the end? Today, the week ends, and the third part of the Bible opens. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

Turn the page past Malachi in a Jewish Bible, and the voices change. A king sings to God on a harp. A father teaches his son, and tells the lazy to go and watch the ant. A man covered in sores argues with heaven and won't be comforted. A woman in love searches the city streets at night. A widow gleans barley behind the harvesters. A queen keeps a secret about who she is. Exiles sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep. And almost no one stands up to say thus saith the LORD. This last part of the Bible has a very plain name.
screen: `A KING SINGS, A FATHER WARNS.` → `A MAN ARGUES, A WOMAN SEARCHES.` → `A WIDOW GLEANS, A QUEEN KEEPS A SECRET.`

segments.voice: Ketuvim. Writings. The Torah is the teaching, the Prophets are the voice of God through messengers, and the Writings are, well, the writings: everything else that was kept. And what's kept is wide. Psalms, the songs and cries that run through the Jewish prayer book. Proverbs, short wisdom about tongues, money and friends. Job, a long argument about suffering that never quite settles. Then a set of short scrolls Jews call megillot, each tied by custom to a season: Song of Songs at Passover, Ruth on Shavuot, Lamentations on Tisha B'Av, Ecclesiastes during Sukkot, Esther on Purim. And then Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah, and Chronicles. Here is what changes when you cross over. In the Prophets, God mostly speaks to people. In the Writings, people mostly speak: to God, to each other, to themselves. They praise, they doubt, they complain, they fall in love, they grieve a city. Ecclesiastes looks at all of it and calls it vanity, all of it. The book of Esther tells its whole story without once naming God. And these books are part of the Bible too. Their questions are kept right next to the answers. One more thing. Printed Bibles don't all list these books in the same order, and the Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, gives an order of its own. It starts with Ruth. Which is where this road goes next. And before it does, look back at a week of endings. Micah's three verbs. A fig tree and no fear. Habakkuk's one line. Not by might. Hearts turning both ways. And a voice that goes on.
screen: `KETUVIM: EVERYTHING ELSE THAT WAS KEPT.` · `PSALMS, PROVERBS, JOB, THE SCROLLS.` · then, large: `HERE, PEOPLE MOSTLY SPEAK.` · then: `THE TALMUD'S ORDER STARTS WITH RUTH.`

segments.voice: The practice is a list: read the names of its books. Settle, and breathe. Then, one name for each slow breath, say them, aloud or inside: Psalms. Proverbs. Job. Song of Songs. Ruth. Lamentations. Ecclesiastes. Esther. Daniel. Ezra. Nehemiah. Chronicles. Notice which name catches you: a song, a lament, a love poem, a story. When you reach the end, go back to the one that caught you and stay with it for the rest of the sit, just the name and the breath. If you pray, you can let one line of a psalm you know be enough. The bell holds the time.
Ketuvim. The Writings, the third part of the Bible, where songs, wisdom and stories speak in human voices. Today's word.
Your line: they praise, they doubt, they complain. Today, write one thing down by hand: a line you want to keep, a worry, a thank-you, a question you can't answer yet. Day eight hundred thirty-three.
